questions.q: Why does "we triaged 4,200 alerts last quarter" fail to land with a board of directors?
options: Boards legally cannot review any security-related numbers
It's an activity count with no trend, no mapped risk, and no decision attached to it
4,200 is too small a number to be worth reporting
Alert triage has nothing to do with security at all
questions.explain: An activity count says the team was busy, not whether risk went up or down, and it doesn't point toward any decision — it fails all three tests a board-grade metric needs to pass.

questions.q: What are the three tests a metric should pass before it belongs on a board-level security report?
options: Is it a trend (not a snapshot), does it map to a risk the board already owns, and does it point toward a decision
Is it measured in dollars, is it under 100 characters, and was it approved by the CISO
Is it a CVSS score, is it from the current quarter, and is it from an automated tool
Is it encrypted, is it backed up, and is it stored in the SIEM
questions.explain: A board-grade metric needs trend context, a connection to a risk category the board already tracks, and an implied action or decision — a single activity count typically has none of the three.

questions.q: Why is "% reduction in critical unpatched systems, trended quarterly against a target" a stronger board metric than a raw vulnerability count?
options: Raw counts are always inaccurate and should never be measured internally
It requires no scanning tools to produce
It is inherently a trend, maps to the risk of exploitation of known vulnerabilities, and tells the board what to ask if the trend reverses
It replaces the need for a CVSS score entirely in every context
questions.explain: The percentage-reduction trend passes all three tests: it has built-in trend context, it connects directly to a risk category the board owns, and a reversal signals exactly what needs attention.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should a "risk acceptance" look like when it's reported to the board?
options: It should never be reported to the board under any circumstances
As an outstanding item with an owner and a review date, especially when it sits above the board's own risk threshold
As a single aggregate number with no further detail
Only as a verbal mention, never in writing
questions.explain: Outstanding risk acceptances above the board's threshold are reported with an owner and review date so the board can see which accepted risks are stale or need re-evaluation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that choosing board-grade metrics is NOT "dumbing down" the message?
options: Because boards actually prefer more technical detail than engineers do
Because it eliminates the need for any risk quantification work
Because a board member is expected to independently translate raw technical data during the meeting

Because doing the translation work in advance is a harder, more disciplined exercise than reporting everything that was measured, and a raw count just shifts that work onto an audience that can't do it well
questions.explain: Handing a board raw technical output is the lazier move — it pushes translation work onto an audience without the time or technical grounding to do it, and the message usually gets lost or misread as a result.
